strengths: Clear, well-formulated diagnostic question that addresses an important puzzle in vision-language models: whether CLIP's bag-of-words (BoW) behavior stems from representational deficits in unimodal encoders or failures in cross-modal alignment.

Convincing unimodal experimental evidence: utilizing linear probing across varying object counts and a conjunctive search task to demonstrate that attribute-object binding information is already encoded in both image and text representations independently.

A remarkably simple yet effective solution (LABCLIP): learning a frozen-encoder linear transformation ($D \times D$) on text embeddings using hard negatives recovers cross-modal binding performance, rivaling full-encoder fine-tuning (NegCLIP) on ARO and SugarCrepe.
High practical relevance: the approach is computationally cheap, backward-compatible with deployed vector databases, and avoids expensive feature re-extraction.

Thorough empirical analysis and ablation in the appendix, including modality gap dynamics, probe weight alignment analysis, and evaluation across multiple CLIP architectures (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14).
weaknesses: Unimodal probing is restricted to synthetic datasets (CLEVR, PUG:SPAR/SPARE): While the authors justify this by the need for exact control over attributes and objects, validating whether real-world complex visual embeddings (e.g., from Visual Genome or COCO) linearly separate bindings to the same degree remains unproven.

Noticeable performance drop on standard zero-shot classification: As shown in Table 11, LABCLIP incurs a significant drop on standard zero-shot recognition benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet top-1 decreases from 56% to 46% when trained on COCO). This trade-off between attribute binding and broad concept categorization warrants more prominent discussion in the main text.

Narrow compositional scope: The study focuses strictly on attribute-object binding; as the authors note in Table 10, the learned alignment does not generalize to other compositional dimensions (such as spatial relationships) without explicit supervision on those relations.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental and well-known shortcoming of vision-language models like CLIP: its apparent bag-of-words (BoW) behavior and failure in attribute-object binding.

The central hypothesis—that CLIP's BoW behavior stems from cross-modal misalignment rather than a lack of unimodal binding information—is conceptually insightful, clearly formulated, and rigorously tested.

The experimental design for unimodal analysis is extensive and persuasive: it includes linear probing on multiple controlled datasets, debiasing positional artifacts (PUG:SPARE), stress-testing with increasing object counts (up to 10 objects), and visual conjunctive search.

The proposed post-hoc remedy (LABCLIP) elegantly supports the core thesis: learning a simple D x D linear projection on frozen text embeddings achieves performance competitive with full encoder fine-tuning (e.g., NegCLIP) on compositional benchmarks (ARO, SugarCrepe) while requiring orders of magnitude fewer parameters and keeping image vector databases intact.
The manuscript is clearly written, logically structured, and provides thorough appendices detailing dataset construction, training setups, and analyses on the modality gap.
weaknesses: Unimodal probing experiments are conducted predominantly on synthetic benchmarks (CLEVR, PUG:SPAR/SPARE). While the controlled setup is justified to prevent confounders, demonstrating similar unimodal linear decodability on natural images (e.g., localized objects in Visual Genome) would further strengthen the claims.

There is a notable trade-off on zero-shot single-object classification: zero-shot ImageNet top-1 accuracy drops from 56% to 46% (COCO-trained) and 51% (CC3M-trained). Further discussion or regularization techniques to mitigate this drop would enhance practical applicability.

While LABCLIP matches or approaches NegCLIP on several compositional benchmarks, NegCLIP still holds an edge on certain relation and order tasks (e.g., Flickr PRC: 0.91 vs. 0.84, COCO PRC: 0.86 vs. 0.81), indicating that full fine-tuning may still capture structural nuances beyond a global linear mapping.

strengths: Clear and insightful research question: The paper cleanly disentangles unimodal representation capacity from cross-modal alignment, providing a fresh and well-motivated perspective on the widely reported 'bag-of-words' (BoW) behavior of CLIP.

Methodologically sound diagnostic experiments: The authors establish unimodal binding through multiple complementary angles, including object-specific linear probing, scaling the number of objects (up to 10), conjunctive search tests, and a necessary sanity check using an explicit BoW-constrained model.

Careful benchmark construction: The authors identify a positional shortcut in PUG:SPAR and construct PUG:SPARE to ensure probing results reflect true attribute-object binding rather than spatial position correlations.

Lightweight, practical solution (LABCLIP): Demonstrating that a single frozen-encoder linear transformation ($D \times D$) can recover cross-modal binding performance competitive with fully fine-tuned models (e.g., NegCLIP) strongly supports the hypothesis while offering practical utility for existing vector databases.
weaknesses: Performance degradation on standard zero-shot classification: As shown in Table 11, LABCLIP suffers noticeable drops in zero-shot classification benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet drops from 0.56 to 0.46 for LABCLIP-COCO). The paper would benefit from exploring regularization or mitigation strategies to preserve general zero-shot classification capabilities.

Evaluation limited to OpenAI CLIP: Experiments are conducted across multiple ViT sizes (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14) but exclusively on OpenAI's pre-trained weights. Evaluating other contrastive vision-language architectures and pre-training datasets (such as SigLIP or OpenCLIP trained on LAION/DataComp) would verify whether this phenomenon is universal to contrastive dual-encoders.

Unimodal probing is restricted to synthetic datasets: While synthetic data (CLEVR, PUG) is justified for controlled ground-truth binding combinations, the absence of unimodal probing on natural/real-world images leaves a gap between synthetic probing conclusions and real-world retrieval evaluations.
